The word temple has two completely separate meanings as a noun. They have nothing to do with each other — they just happen to share the same spelling.

A temple is a building where people go to worship a god or multiple gods. It is considered a sacred (holy) place — meaning it is set apart from ordinary life and treated with deep respect.

Think of it as a building that acts as a home for a deity, or as a meeting point between humans and the divine. People visit temples to pray, offer gifts, perform rituals, seek blessings, meditate, or simply to feel connected to something greater than themselves.

Which religions use the word "temple"?

This is important, because not every religion calls its place of worship a "temple."

  • Hinduism — Hindu places of worship are called temples. They typically house statues (called idols or murtis) of gods and goddesses. Rituals, offerings of flowers and food, the ringing of bells, and the burning of incense are common there.
  • Buddhism — Buddhist temples are places of meditation, reflection, and reverence for the Buddha. They often contain statues of the Buddha and are spaces of quiet and peace.
  • Sikhism — The Sikh place of worship is called a Gurdwara, but it is sometimes informally referred to as a temple in everyday speech.
  • Ancient religions — The ancient Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians built grand temples dedicated to their gods. For example, the Parthenon in Athens was a temple dedicated to the goddess Athena. These are now mostly historical or archaeological sites.
  • Judaism — The most famous temple in Jewish history is the Temple in Jerusalem (also called Solomon's Temple or the Second Temple), which was the holiest site in ancient Judaism. Modern Jewish places of worship are usually called synagogues, though some Jewish communities do call them temples.
  • The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS) — This Christian denomination does call its sacred buildings "temples." These are considered especially holy and are used for specific religious ceremonies.
  • Islam — The Muslim place of worship is called a mosque, not a temple.
  • Christianity (most denominations) — Christians generally use words like church, cathedral, or chapel, not temple.

So in everyday English, when someone says "temple," the listener most naturally pictures a Hindu or Buddhist place of worship, or an ancient historical structure. Context usually makes the specific religion clear.

A temple is not just any religious building. It often carries a sense of grandeur, permanence, and deep holiness. When a temple is very famous or ancient, it can also become a cultural landmark that people visit for its history, art, and architecture — even those who are not religious.

Examples in sentences:

  • She lit incense and left flowers at the entrance of the temple.
  • The ancient Greek temples on the hilltop have stood for over 2,000 years.
  • Every morning, the monks gathered at the temple to meditate.
Meaning 2: A Part of the Human Head

The second meaning of temple is a specific part of your body.

Your temples are the flat, slightly soft areas on either side of your head — located between your forehead (at the front) and your ear (at the side). If you place your fingertips on the sides of your head, just beside your eyes and above your cheekbones, you are touching your temples.

This is the area where people often press or rub their fingers when they have a headache. It is also where you can sometimes feel a faint pulse (a throb or beat), because a blood vessel called the temporal artery runs just beneath the skin there.

The word is almost always used in the plural (temples) because there are two of them — one on each side of the head.

As people age, the temples are often one of the first places where grey or white hair appears. You might hear phrases like "grey at the temples" to describe someone who has started going grey in that area but still has darker hair elsewhere.

Examples in sentences:

  • He rubbed his temples, trying to ease his headache.
  • She had silver hair at her temples, though the rest was still dark.
  • The doctor noticed a vein pulsing visibly at his temple.

The word "temple" (Meaning 1) is also used figuratively in a common and well-known phrase:

"Your body is a temple."

This expression means that your body is sacred and deserves to be treated with care and respect — just as a holy temple is maintained with reverence. It is used to encourage people to eat well, exercise, avoid harmful substances, and generally take good care of their physical selves.
How to Tell the Meanings Apart in Context

Since the two meanings are so different, context always makes it obvious:

  • If someone is talking about religion, worship, buildings, gods, ancient history, or spirituality → they mean the place of worship.
  • If someone is talking about the head, headaches, hair, anatomy, or the body → they mean the part of the skull.

You will never confuse the two in real usage because they belong to entirely different conversations.
